DGM: Why Is Morocco Seeing Extreme Heat and Intense Storms in September?
Morocco experienced a sharp shift in weather at the start of September, with extreme heat occurring alongside powerful thunderstorms in several regions.
Casablanca – Morocco’s weather changed noticeably at the beginning of September after a hot August, according to the General Directorate of Meteorology (DGM). The month began with a combination of exceptionally high temperatures and, at times, intense thunderstorm activity.
August brought persistent heat, particularly to Morocco’s inland areas, the southeast and the Saharan provinces. At the start of September, however, several atmospheric factors came together and produced a more unstable weather pattern.
According to DGM’s “Weather Overview for Early September 2026 in Morocco,” the expansion of the Saharan thermal low toward the north, accompanied by southerly to southeasterly winds, pushed very hot air toward Morocco’s inland regions.
The Chergui winds also played a role, while pockets of colder air moved into the upper atmosphere.
At the same time, warm and humid tropical air masses moved into the middle layers of the atmosphere. This increased the amount of water vapor in the air and made the heat feel more intense, particularly along coastal areas and the Atlantic plains.
The combination of these conditions with the effect of Morocco’s mountains created favorable conditions for thunderstorms, especially during the afternoons and early evenings over the High Atlas and Middle Atlas mountain ranges and nearby areas. Some of the storm cells brought heavy hail and strong wind gusts.
The DGM said the weather pattern also explains why thunderstorms can form while temperatures remain very high at ground level. Heat provides the energy needed for convection, while tropical humidity supplies additional moisture that allows convective clouds to develop rapidly.
The heat reached exceptional levels on September 3rd. Sidi Slimane recorded 47.1 C, while Kenitra reached 45.1 C and Sale recorded 44.3 C, setting new September records in the respective provinces.
The meteorological agency described September as a transition period, when summer influences such as Saharan heat and tropical air can interact with the first incursions of cooler air at higher altitudes.
This interaction can create strong temperature contrasts and contribute to intense weather events, according to the agency.

Parents raise alarms about sweltering Long Beach classrooms during extreme heat wave
Hand-held fans, donated swamp coolers and popsicles are just a few of the stopgap measures Long Beach students, parents and teachers have employed to keep cool recently on campuses without air conditioning.
After multiple sweltering heatwaves since school began in August, some parents say they’re tired of sending their kids into hot classrooms — even keeping their kids home to stay cool.
Although 90% of Long Beach Unified schools are fully air-conditioned, eight campuses are still awaiting updated HVAC systems, expected to be completed by the end of 2027, with the exception of Poly High School, which will be completed the following year. Amid record-breaking temperatures that reached 107 degrees this week, parents and teachers told the Long Beach Post that students’ health and education are suffering at schools without air conditioning.
Six parents and teachers reached out to the Post to discuss health and educational concerns related to the heat. They described stifling classrooms, limited access to cooling stations and a lack of clarity about how student and staff safety would be protected.
The Long Beach Unified School District issued a heat mitigation memo this week, which said that students and teachers had access to chilled water dispensers, portable fans and shade structures. The memo also said that strenuous activity would shift to cooler hours, students would be encouraged to drink water and rooms without AC would be ventilated.
Eight Long Beach Unified schools are still awaiting air-conditioning: Millikan High School, Poly High School, Sato Academy, Hoover Middle School, Marshall Academy, Carver Elementary, Henry Elementary and Los Cerritos Elementary
Yet those measures haven’t prevented the effects of heat, parents said. Katie Jakemer, a parent of a student at Henry, has noticed the physical toll on her daughter, who has expressed anxiety and dread about the heat at school, Jakemer said. “If you have a kid that comes home red-faced, falling asleep at the dinner table, has headaches, you can’t just stay quiet,” she said.
On Tuesday, she posted a video to Instagram expressing her frustration that students are being asked to sit in blistering temperatures and urging the district to consider modifying the school day.
LBUSD spokesperson Eric Mitchell said schools would only close for extreme weather if directed to by city, county or state authorities. He said the district has nothing further to add about why it made that decision.
The state’s funding formula incentivizes Long Beach Unified and other districts to keep kids in class even on hot days. The district loses approximately $75 for each day a student isn’t in class, according to a December budget update.
Yet the heat may be affecting attendance anyway. The district’s attendance tracker on Thursday showed it dipped by about one percentage point over the last five school days when compared to overall attendance since school began.
The effect is slightly more pronounced at some campuses without air conditioning, including Patrick Henry and Carver Elementary Schools, which each dipped by about 1.5% from their respective baselines.
Miguel Lozada, whose child attends Henry Elementary, bought a $330 swamp cooler, which he donated to the school, according to an email reviewed by the Post. But the cooler was only used for a day before Lozada was told he needed to come pick it up, he said. He still doesn’t understand why.
Parents and teachers said the heat was directly affecting learning. One parent said her son had to undergo standardized testing without air conditioning on some of the hottest days, and she worried he had underperformed as a result.
Annette Quintero, a teacher at Poly High School, said that even though her classroom is air-conditioned, students must walk outdoors across campus during passing periods. Some arrived tired and angry after sleeping poorly in the heat, Quintero said. “I’ve seen more heads down in the last few days.”
Experts have warned these hot days may soon be the norm. The mild, dry summers that Southern California has historically enjoyed — thanks to a protective marine layer, cool ocean temperatures and a high-pressure system — may be in jeopardy as meteorological patterns are disrupted by climate change, the Los Angeles Times reported.
According to Long Beach’s Climate Change Assessment, the city could experience an average of 11 to 16 days of extreme heat (above 95 degrees) by midcentury. Southern California was not built for this, and many homes and buildings still lack air conditioning — though Long Beach Unified is racing to catch up.
Quintero has spoken before the school board in the past, urging them to consider a more proactive approach to extreme weather days, similar to how some districts cancel school for heavy snow, she said.
Long Beach will continue to experience extreme weather, from poor air quality to fire to heat, she said. “Given climate change, we need to have policies on the books” — ones that address problems proactively, not reactively, she said.
Editor’s note: This story was corrected to show Quintero said students must walk outdoors to get to other classes, not that they must attend some classes outdoors.
by
Kate Raphael
Kate Raphael is a California Local News Fellow. She covers education for the Long Beach Post.

Effects of extreme heat
The most frequently cited effects were:
- increased fatigue or difficulty concentrating (39 per cent)
Calls for government action
|
# |
Danger |
Description |
Source |
|
1 |
Heat exhaustion and heat stroke |
The Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety notes that heat stress causes a spectrum of disorders ranging from heat rash and cramps to life-threatening heat exhaustion and heat stroke. Heat stroke, the most severe form, can cause irreversible damage to the heart, lungs, kidneys and liver if not treated immediately. |
Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety (via IHSA), "Heat Stress"; Sun Safety at Work Canada study, BMC |
|
2 |
Acute and chronic kidney injury |
A 2025 review in the Journal of Climate Change and Health found that outdoor workers face significant risk of acute kidney injury and chronic interstitial nephritis from repeated heat exposure and dehydration, estimating roughly 4.8 million U.S. outdoor workers experience heat-related kidney strain. A separate Thai cohort study found men with prolonged occupational heat exposure were 2.22 times more likely to develop kidney disease than unexposed workers. |
Werner, Carrion & Huguet, "Risk for renal injury from heat-related stress among outdoor workers," Journal of Climate Change and Health, 2025; Science.gov summary of occupational heat stress and kidney disease cohort study |
|
3 |
Cardiovascular strain and cardiac events |
Research led by Dr. Daniel Gagnon found that even a 0.5°C rise in core body temperature triggered myocardial ischemia in over a third of older adults with coronary artery disease during passive heat exposure, despite no symptoms of angina. Heat exposure increases cardiac output and workload as the body redirects blood flow to the skin to cool down, placing added strain on the heart. |
Gagnon, "Exposure to heat has significant effects on the heart," Observatoire de prévention, July 17, 2024 |
|
4 |
Cognitive impairment and elevated accident risk |
The American Industrial Hygiene Association reports that heat can reduce the brain function responsible for reasoning, while sweaty palms, fogged safety glasses and dizziness create additional safety hazards on the job. A 2025 comment package submitted to OSHA by the American College of Occupational and Environmental Medicine cited research showing occupational injury rates rose by nearly 10 per cent with increases in workplace temperature. |
"Heat Hazards," The Synergist, AIHA; ACOEM Comment Package, Occupational Heat Standard, submitted to OSHA, Jan. 13, 2025 |
|
5 |
Rhabdomyolysis and heat-related burns |
Rhabdomyolysis, the breakdown of injured muscle tissue that releases proteins and electrolytes into the bloodstream, can be triggered by excessive heat and may cause serious harm to the kidneys and heart. Workers also face burn risks from contact with hot surfaces, steam or equipment, an additional hazard flagged separately by NIOSH-based safety guidance. |
"Working in Heat: A Summary of CCOHS, Albertan, and OSHA Recommendations"; Maryland Occupational Safety and Health (MOSH), "Heat Stress" |

- IMD Issues Yellow Alert for Mumbai With Rain Forecast on September 12-13
Trending
Mumbai: The IMD has forecast a yellow alert for Mumbai, Thane, and Palghar on September 12 and 13, warning of thunderstorms with lightning, light to moderate rainfall, and gusty winds of 30-40 kmph at isolated places.On September 14, the first day of Ganpati, Mumbai is expected to see moderate rain, while on September 15, the first day of idol immersions, the city is likely to receive light to moderate rainfall.Since June 1 this year, the IMD’s Colaba observatory has recorded 1,809.9 mm of rainfall, while the Santacruz observatory has recorded 2,259.9 mm. With little or no rain recorded over the past few days, Colaba has now started showing a rainfall departure, with the cumulative figure standing at 4.3 mm below normal. Santacruz, meanwhile, is currently 7 mm above normal.The normal date for the withdrawal of the southwest monsoon from Mumbai is October 8. Last year, withdrawal was declared exactly a week later, on October 15. In 2024, the withdrawal was delayed further, with the IMD declaring it on October 23.
